title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

topics.title: Electrons and how they escape metals

learn.hook: The solar panels on rooftops from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu rely on light knocking electrons free. To understand them, we start with the electron itself.
points: J.J. Thomson (1897), studying cathode rays in discharge tubes, showed they are streams of negatively charged particles, electrons, and measured their charge-to-mass ratio e/m. Millikan's oil-drop experiment measured the charge e (about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
This raised a deep question: do light and matter have both wave and particle character?
Free electrons in a metal cannot normally leave its surface; they are held by the attraction of the positive ions. Extra energy is needed to pull them out.

Work function φ₀: the minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal surface, usually given in eV (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). It depends on the metal and its surface; caesium has a low value (about 2.14 eV) and platinum a high one (about 5.65 eV).
Ways to supply this energy: thermionic emission (heating), field emission (very strong electric field, about 10⁸ V m⁻¹), and photoelectric emission (light of suitable frequency).

example.q: A metal has a work function of 2.3 eV. Express it in joules.

learn.reallife: Old television picture tubes and the X-ray tubes at Indian diagnostic centres use thermionic emission: a heated filament boils off electrons.

Electrons in a metal are free inside but cannot leave freely

learn.hook: In 1887, Heinrich Hertz noticed that sparks jumped more easily when ultraviolet light shone on his metal electrodes. He had stumbled on the photoelectric effect.
points: Hertz (1887): ultraviolet light falling on the spark gap made high-voltage sparks pass more easily.
Hallwachs and Lenard (1886–1902): UV light on a zinc plate releases negatively charged particles (electrons). A negatively charged zinc plate loses its charge, while a neutral one becomes positive.
There is a threshold frequency ν₀: below it no electrons are emitted, however intense the light.
Alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium, rubidium) emit electrons even with visible light; zinc, cadmium and magnesium need ultraviolet. Such materials are called photosensitive.

Experimental set-up: an evacuated glass tube with a photosensitive plate (emitter, cathode C) and a collector (anode A), a variable potential difference between them, a microammeter, and a monochromatic light source through a quartz window.

example.q: A neutral zinc plate on an electroscope is exposed to UV light. What happens to the leaves and why?
steps: UV ejects electrons from the zinc.

example.answer: The leaves diverge because the plate becomes positively charged

learn.reallife: The automatic doors at Indian metro stations and malls once used photocells: light falling on a photosensitive surface gave a current, and blocking the beam changed it.

learn.hook: Turn up the brightness of the light in a photocell and the current rises. But the fastest electrons do not get any faster. That surprised everyone.
points: For a frequency above threshold, the photocurrent (and number of electrons emitted per second) is directly proportional to the intensity of light.
As the anode's positive potential increases, the photocurrent rises and then levels off: the saturation current, when all emitted electrons are collected.
Making the anode negative reduces the current; at the stopping potential V₀ (cut-off), even the fastest electrons are stopped and the current becomes zero. Then Kmax = eV₀.
For a given frequency, the stopping potential is the same for all intensities; only the saturation current changes.
Emission is instantaneous: electrons come out within about 10⁻⁹ s of the light being switched on, even for very dim light.

example.q: The stopping potential for a metal is 1.5 V. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in eV and J.

learn.reallife: Light meters in cameras and the automatic street lights switched on at dusk in many Indian towns use the fact that photocurrent grows with light intensity.

topics.title: Effect of frequency, and why wave theory failed

learn.hook: Classical physics said: make the light bright enough and electrons will fly out at any colour. Experiments said no. Something had to give.
points: For a given metal, the stopping potential V₀ increases linearly with the frequency ν of the incident light.
A graph of V₀ against ν is a straight line cutting the ν-axis at the threshold frequency ν₀. Below ν₀, no emission.
For different metals, the lines are parallel (the same slope, h/e), but they have different threshold frequencies.
Wave theory predicted that Kmax should increase with intensity, since a brighter wave carries more energy. Experiment shows Kmax depends only on frequency.
Wave theory also could not explain the existence of a threshold frequency or why emission is instantaneous (it predicted a long delay for dim light while energy builds up).

example.q: For a metal, V₀ = 0 at ν = 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz and V₀ = 2 V at ν = 10 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find the slope h/e.
example.answer: 4 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s (so h = slope × e ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻³⁴ J s from these data, close to the accepted 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

learn.reallife: Physicists at India's Raman Research Institute in Bengaluru and elsewhere still teach this experiment as the moment classical physics broke and quantum physics was born.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why couldn't the wave picture of light explain the photoelectric effect?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Wave theory couldn't explain the threshold frequency, why Kmax ignores intensity, or why emission is instant. Time for photons!
teach.nudge: Good! Name the observations that went against the wave picture.

revise.summary: Stopping potential rises linearly with frequency; the V₀–ν line has slope h/e for every metal and cuts the axis at the threshold frequency. Wave theory failed to explain the threshold, the frequency dependence of Kmax and instant emission.
remember: Slope h/e same for all metals; intercept ν₀
traps: Lines for different metals are parallel, not identical
Kmax does not depend on intensity, as wave theory wrongly predicted

learn.hook: In 1905 Einstein proposed that light comes in packets of energy. One equation then explained everything the wave theory could not, and won him the Nobel Prize.
points: Light consists of quanta (photons), each of energy E = hν, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (Planck's constant). One photon is absorbed by one electron.
Einstein's equation: Kmax = hν - φ₀ = eV₀.
Threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h; threshold wavelength λ₀ = c/ν₀ = hc/φ₀. No emission if ν < ν₀ (or λ > λ₀).

This explains: threshold (photon energy must exceed φ₀); Kmax rising linearly with ν; intensity affecting only the number of photons (and so the current); instantaneous emission (one photon, one electron, no waiting).
Millikan's careful experiments verified the equation; the slope h/e of the V₀-ν graph gave a value of h close to Planck's.

example.q: Light of frequency 1.2 × 10¹⁵ Hz falls on a metal with φ₀ = 3 eV. Find Kmax and V₀. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

learn.reallife: Solar cells on ISRO's satellites and on Indian rooftops work on the photon idea: each absorbed photon with enough energy frees one electron to drive a current.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did Einstein explain why light below a certain frequency can't eject electrons?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Each photon carries energy hν. If hν is less than the work function, no single photon can free an electron! Quantum!

revise.summary: Einstein treated light as photons of energy hν, each absorbed by one electron: Kmax = hν − φ₀ = eV₀. Threshold frequency is φ₀/h and threshold wavelength hc/φ₀, explaining all photoelectric observations; Millikan confirmed it.
focus: How the equation explains the observations
remember: ν₀ = φ₀/h; λ₀ = hc/φ₀; hc ≈ 1240 eV nm
traps: Intensity changes photon number, not photon energy

learn.hook: Is a photon a particle? It has energy and momentum, travels at c, but has no rest mass. Here is the photon's identity card.
points: Typical problem 1: given λ and φ₀, find Kmax = hc/λ - φ₀ and V₀ = Kmax/e. Handy value: hc ≈ 1240 eV nm.
Typical problem 2: given V₀ at two frequencies, find h/e from the slope, then φ₀ and ν₀.
Photon properties: energy E = hν = hc/λ; momentum p = hν/c = h/λ; speed c in vacuum; zero rest mass.
The intensity of light at a given frequency is proportional to the number of photons crossing unit area per second, not to the energy of each photon.
Bright red light has many low-energy photons; dim violet light can have fewer but more energetic photons.

learn.reallife: LED lights promoted under India's UJALA scheme emit photons whose energies are set by the semiconductor material, giving different colours at very high efficiency.

topics.title: Photons in collisions and photon counting

learn.hook: A 1 W LED glows with billions of billions of photons every second. Counting them is as simple as dividing power by the energy of one photon.
points: Photons are electrically neutral, so they are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
In photon-particle collisions (such as photon-electron collisions), total energy and total momentum are conserved, but the number of photons need not be: photons can be absorbed or created.
Number of photons emitted per second by a source of power P at wavelength λ: n = P/(hν) = Pλ/(hc).
Photon energy E = hν = hc/λ; photon momentum p = h/λ.
For a fixed power, shorter-wavelength (higher-energy) light means fewer photons per second.

learn.hook: If light waves can act like particles, can particles act like waves? A young Louis de Broglie said yes in 1924, and electrons proved him right.
points: de Broglie hypothesis: a moving particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength λ = h/p = h/(mv).
For everyday objects λ is unimaginably tiny (a cricket ball's is about 10⁻³⁴ m), so no wave effects are seen. For electrons, λ is comparable to atomic spacings, so wave effects are clear.
In terms of kinetic energy K: λ = h/√(2mK). For an electron accelerated through V volts: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.227/√V nm.
Wave-particle duality: both radiation and matter show wave and particle aspects, but not both in the same measurement.
Electron microscopes use the very short de Broglie wavelength of fast electrons to resolve details far smaller than optical microscopes can.

example.q: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V.

learn.reallife: Electron microscopes at IISc Bengaluru and other Indian research centres image viruses and nanomaterials using electrons whose de Broglie wavelength is far shorter than visible light's.

learn.hook: Electrons, neutrons and photons: each has a wavelength, and quantum problems often ask you to compare them. A few formulas cover them all.
points: Particle with speed v: λ = h/(mv). With kinetic energy K: λ = h/√(2mK).
Electron accelerated through V volts: λ = 1.227/√V nm. Doubling V divides λ by √2.
Photon: E = hc/λ and p = h/λ. For a photon and an electron of the same wavelength, their momenta are equal, but their energies differ.
Slow (thermal) neutrons from reactors have de Broglie wavelengths of the order of 0.1 nm, comparable to atomic spacings, so they are used to study crystals.
Comparing particles: at the same speed, λ ∝ 1/m; at the same kinetic energy, λ ∝ 1/√m; for the same accelerating voltage V and charge q, λ ∝ 1/√(mq).

example.q: An electron and a photon both have λ = 1 nm. Compare their momenta, and find the photon's energy. (hc = 1240 eV nm)
steps: p = h/λ is the same for both
